title: The impact of photovoltaic projects on ecological corridors through the Least-Cost Path model
abstract:
With the dramatic development of photovoltaic power in China, its side effect on the ecological
system has generally been attention to and systematically studied. This paper aims to analyze the potential impacts of PV projects on ecological networks through the quantitative assessment of the changes in the patency, length, and connection strength of the ecological corridors under scenarios with and without PV projects. The least-cost distance and least-cost path models are utilized in this research to establish the ecological corridors with ecological sources and resistance
surfaces. The research is conducted at the proposed PV sites of Huabu Town and its surrounding areas in Quzhou City, Zhejiang Province, in East China. The PV project site selection procedures are also introduced in the research framework to determine the site under multi-factor decisionmaking. The results showed that PV projects could have various impacts on ecological corridors on a larger spatial scale, primarily resulting in decreased corridor patency and connection strength. Contrary to the previous research findings, the length of corridors is universally reduced due to the PV projects for prediction, which can guide the site selection with consideration of the
regional ecological system protection. Through GIS spatial quantification research, this paper
helps balance photovoltaic development and regional ecological security. It provides scientific and orderly planning suggestions for the healthy development of the regional ecological network. At the same time, it provides method reference and data support for PV site selection and ecological impact assessment in mountainous areas.

## **1. Introduction**

Climate change, environmental pollution, ecological damage, and other issues brought about by the large-scale development and utilization of fossil energy have aroused public concern. In 2019, China generated around 33% of the world’s carbon emissions (Anon, 2021), and the challenge of cutting emissions is still pressing. In September 2020, the Chinese government promised to reach the carbon emissions peak before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. With the continuous expansion of photovoltaic power, the consecutive progress of technology, and the accelerating cost decline, photovoltaic power has become the main force of new power investment. Vigorously developing photovoltaic power generation is a crucial way to achieve the goal of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, build a new power system, and achieve green and low-carbon energy transformation.

With the installation of photovoltaic power reaching a new record of 54.88 GW in 2021, the cumulative capacity of photovoltaic

power in China has exceeded 300 GW by the end of 2021, ranking first worldwide for seven years. The generating capacity continued ⋅ to improve, reaching 325.9 billion kW h, up 25.1% from 2020. The average utilization hours for PV generation was 1163 h and the utilization rate of power generation remained at a relatively high level, at 98%. Distributed PV was prominent, with the new installed capacity of 29.28 GW, up 84% and accounting for 53.4% of all new PV installed capacity. The development trend of centralized and distributed photovoltaic power generation is noticeable (Anon, 2022).

China is rich in solar energy resources. The annual horizontal radiation in most areas is more than 1000 kWh/m[2] , and the annual sunshine duration is more than 2000 h in over 2/3 of the regions (Anon, 2022). Since China proposed the carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals, the local authorities have actively responded to the central government with practical implementation resolutions. Zhejiang, Shandong, Jiangsu, Inner Mongolia, Gansu, and Xinjiang have implemented new energy development plans in their 14th Five-Year Plan and 2035 goals. The State Council has clarified that by 2030, the cumulative installed capacity of wind and solar power will reach 1200 GW. The annual installed capacity of photovoltaic power generation is expected to exceed 140 GW from 2025 to 2030 and 300 GW from 2030 to 2060 (Anon, 2022).

However, photovoltaic projects have potential adverse ecological and environmental impacts, which should not be neglected. Their long-term impacts on the ecological system could pose critical threats to the energy transition and carbon neutrality target. Scientific, systematic, and quantitative research is urgently needed to guarantee a balanced relationship between environmental protection and renewable energy development.

The research on photovoltaic planning and construction started earlier in western countries, and its negative consequences on the physical environment have received much attention (Abbasi and Abbasi, 2000). PV project infrastructure may fragment habitats and serve as linear barriers to the movement patterns of certain wildlife species. Therefore, PV projects are recognized as the greatest threat to biological diversity. The reflection and glare from PV panels can affect the vision of road users. However, at present, typical polysilicon solar cells are used in China. The outer layer is special toughened glass, and the reflectivity is only 5%, which will not cause obvious light pollution (ZHANG, 2021). Infrastructure components may exacerbate or cause a fire, soil compaction, and dust. The concentration of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus elements, and organic matter in soil decreased while heavy metal ions increased. Some noise affects the surrounding residents (Guerin, 2017). During construction, dust kicks up and pollutes the atmosphere (Guerin, 2017; Zarzavilla et al., 2022). The real environmental advantage of downwind PM emission reduction from a utility-scale PV plant owing to wind sheltering is also present in desert conditions (Ravikumar and Sinha, 2017). In the operation phase, a large number of dust suppressants and water are utilized to clean the panels and prevent dust generation for PV plants, which might cause adverse impacts on fauna and flora in the long term (Abbasi and Abbasi, 2000; Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Hernandez et al., 2014).

With the dramatic growth of PV capacity in China, attention to the environmental impact caused by massive PV power stations has also been steadily raised, especially in ecologically sensitive regions. Although environmental impact assessment is compulsory for PV projects during the planning process, the potential influences on the ecological network and service are largely oversimplified or even ignored. There is a lack of data collection, theoretical innovation, and empirical methods to quantitatively assess the impact of PV power on the ecosystem at the regional scale. Intense biomass harvesting could reduce forest sequestering carbon and its natural hazard protection function. Martínez-Martínez et al.’s finding (Martínez-Martínez et al., 2022) provides a better understanding of local renewable energy development and can help implement energy planning and forest management. Wind energy development also has impacted the environment, particularly wildlife and the habitats that support it. Copping et al (Copping et al., 2020). establish a framework for adapting ecosystem-based management to wind energy development which may offer regulators insights into better siting and consenting procedures. In addition, unconventional gas and wind energy substantially impact land use, affecting wildlife populations and ecosystem services. Davis et al. (2018) incorporate ecosystem services into analyses to provide a more accurate and realistic assessment of the value of these new energy developments to urge governments and regulatory agencies to be aware of these impacts and develop appropriate oversight and legal frameworks.

This study made the effort to fill the gap in research regarding the impact of photovoltaic projects on ecological corridors in Zhejiang Province through the least-cost path (LCP) model. The main research aims of the study are: (1) to estimate the effects on corridor patency, corridor length, and connection strength by comparing the lowest cost distance and lowest cost path of ecological corridors before and after photovoltaic construction; and (2) to give constructive instructions for the site selection of future photovoltaic projects.

Huabu Town and its surrounding areas in Kaihua County, Quzhou City, Zhejiang Province were selected as the research area. Zhejiang provincial government has encouraged the development of photovoltaic power projects and provided policy subsidies. It is estimated that 207.5 GW of photovoltaic power will be installed in Zhejiang by 2025, doubling the current installed capacity. There is foreseeable ecological degradation in mountain areas of Zhejiang due to PV development. In June 2022, the Ministry of Natural Resources issued the latest official document announcing that the permits for photovoltaic power projects should be strictly limited and prohibited site selection on arable land and areas within the ecological protection red line. Through GIS spatial quantification research, this paper helps balance photovoltaic development and regional ecological security, and provides scientific and orderly planning suggestions for the healthy development of the regional ecological network. At the same time, it provides method reference and data support for PV site selection and ecological impact assessment in mountainous areas.

## **2. Method**

## _2.1. Study area_

The study area covers a total area of 3192.06 km[2] (117[◦] 57’− 118[◦] 50’E and 28[◦] 40’− 29[◦] 13’N). As shown in Fig. 1, it spans two

**Fig. 1.** The study area in Huabu Town, Zhejiang Province, China.

provinces, Zhejiang and Jiangxi. It includes 29 township-level administrative divisions, of which 27 are in Zhejiang and two in Jiangxi. The expansion of the research area around Huabu Town is due to the uncertainty in ecologically affected areas of PV projects. The research area enjoys a subtropical monsoon climate rich in red and yellow soils. It is mainly distributed in subtropical evergreen broadleaved forests. The area has complex and diverse ecosystems, with extensive green spaces and vegetation providing a cradle for the development of biodiversity. Zhejiang Provincial Government aims to achieve a clean, low-carbon, safe, and efficient energy and circular economy system in 2060. This study focuses on the site selection of photovoltaic projects in Huabu Town and their associated ecological impacts following Zhejiang Province’s low-carbon development targets. In terms of economic benefits and low-carbon energy development, establishing complementary agricultural and optical projects in Huabu Town can contribute to win-win outcomes. However, from an ecological standpoint, the proposed photovoltaic base may potentially threaten the surrounding ecological corridors.

## _2.2. Data sources_

The Geospatial Data Cloud (http://www.gscloud.cn/search) provided Landsat TM images with a resolution of 30 m during the – study period of 2014 2020. Based on Landsat 8, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) in 2014 and 2020 were analyzed, respectively. By comparing the difference between near-infrared light, which is highly reflected by vegetation, and the light absorbed in red, the NDVI can be used to determine the amount of green vegetation in a pixel. More green vegetation is present in the pixel when the NDVI value is higher. Landsat TM images from 2014 and 2020 were used to identify various land use types. The slope and slope aspect were processed through the Global Digital Elevation Model (GDEM), obtaining from the Geospatial Data Cloud (https://www. gscloud.cn/search), with a spatial resolution of 30 m. Scenic spots, residential areas, water, and roads were obtained from OpenStreetMap (https://www.openstreetmap.org).

## _2.3. Methods_

This paper aims to assess the impact of PV projects on ecological corridors through the least-cost path model. It follows the research framework as illustrated in Fig. 2. First, the source patches in the LCP model are identified through variation trend analysis of NDVI between 2014 and 2020. Second, resistance surfaces are synthesized based on the variations under two scenarios (with and without PV

**Fig. 2.** Research framework.

projects). Third, ecological corridors were generated based on the LCD and LCP model derived from the source and destination patches, and the resistance surface. Finally, the effects of PV projects on the ecological networks were assessed based on corridor patency, length, and connection strength. The section of PV project site selection acts as the reference group for assessing the corridors’ impacts.

## _2.3.1. Determination of PV location_

Based on previous research and local conditions (Al Garni and Awasthi, 2018; Nebey et al., 2020; Tahri et al., 2015), the criteria chosen to select the PV project sites are summarized into four categories: land cover, orography, location, and accessibility. With fieldwork and in-depth analysis, the criteria are further subdivided into eight factors: land cover (Tahri et al., 2015; Uyan, 2013), slope (Tahri et al., 2015; Günen, 2021; Rediske et al., 2020), slope aspect (Tahri et al., 2015; Günen, 2021), distance to village level scenic spots, distance to provincial and city level scenic spots, distance to the residential areas (Uyan, 2013), distance to water and accessibility of roads (Uyan, 2013). Table 1 summarizes the relative values of each factor, attached with classification explanation. The values range from 1 to 100 present the suitability for PV projects construction. Score 1 means high suitability, and vice versa.

## _2.3.2. Selection of source patches_

In landscape ecology, sources are fundamental units with positive net reproduction, which can promote the ecological process (Lomolino, 1988; Guo et al., 2020). Previous scholars usually assigned protected areas and scenic spots as ecological sources, which was subjective and lacked consideration of time variation. In this study, the spatio-temporal variation of NDVI is analyzed to represent the ecological stability of different regions. The pixels with an increasing trend in the NDVI connected to a continuous area were identified as the sources and delineated with a closed curve to analyze the species migratory process in the areas with good vegetation

## _2.3.3. Construction of resistance surfaces_

For comparison, two resistance surfaces are built: one affected by PV siting and one that is not. The former is made up of seven factors: slope, vegetation coverage, land cover, national and provincial roads, county and township roads, relief, and PV selection area (Table 2). Compared to the former, the latter lacks one influencing factor: the PV selection area. The indicator set for resistance surface can be categorized into natural environment and human activities. The indicators of vegetation coverage, relief, and slope fall in the category of natural environment. Indicators in the category of human activities include land used, the buffer zone of different road levels and PV projects (only in the first scenario).

The corresponding NDVI values of 0.5% and 99.5% are used as the values of _NNDVIsoil_ and _NNDVIveg_ .

## _2.3.4. Establishment of ecological corridors by least-cost distance and least-cost path_

The LCP model is a practical method for simulating the landscape ecological process and identifying the most efficient biological migration route (Girvetz and Greco, 2007). The LCP can reflect the spatial trend of species migration with the least cumulative cost during species’ extension (Guo et al., 2020). The LCD and LCP models are widely used to evaluate the ecological function and landscape quality through ecological flow analysis and illustrate the landscape spatial patterns (Balbi et al., 2019). In this study, the ecological corridors were established through the LCD and LCP models performed in ArcGIS 10.8. The previously derived source patches and resistance surface were entered into the LCD model to determine the cumulative resistance value from each pixel to the closest source. The LCP found a single least-cost path connecting every two source patches due to additional calculations based on the LCD and cumulative resistance value. The prospective ecological corridors were these routes.

The strength of the source-to-source connection can be used to characterize the effectiveness of potential ecological corridors and the importance of connecting source patches (Yaping and Haiwei, 2016). The relative importance of ecological corridors was

## **3. Results**

## _3.1. Site selection for PV power projects_

In order to select the best locations that could host a PV power project, eight factors were considered. The outcomes of site selection are shown in Fig. 3. After calculating the sum of each factor’s value, the value of the study area ranged from 8 to 800, representing the suitability for PV project construction. The lower the score, the higher the suitability, and vice versa. Within the administrative area of Huabu Town, four sites suitable for developing PV projects were finally selected.

## _3.2. Least-cost path model_

Areas with absolute change rates of NDVI values from 2014 to 2020 not exceeding 6% (| _S_ | | ≤ 0.06) were selected, and fifteen ecological sources were identified in the study area. Potential ecological corridors that connect every two ecological sources with and

## _3.2.1. Identification of ecological sources_

The spatial distribution of the fifteen ecological sources (Fig. 4) is uneven and more densely distributed marginally in the northwest and southwest of the study area. Only one of the sources with a large area is distributed in the interior of the research scope. From the area of the fifteen ecological sources, small patches ( _<_ 0.5 km[2] ) account for a minor proportion, with a ratio of 6.67%. Medium patches (0.5–2.5 km[2] ) and large patches (2.5–5 km[2] ) account for the most significant proportion of 80%. Super large patches ( _>_ 5 km[2] ) are distributed in the middle and the east of the study site, which also means that the distribution density of the ecological sources decreases from west to east.

## _3.2.2. Construction of ecological resistance surfaces_

According to the distribution of the resistance value, the high resistance areas are mainly situated in the centralized location of roads and buildings. It can be seen from the comparison of the two figures (Fig. 5) that Photovoltaic projects have brought about the expansion of the high resistance surface area in the center of the study area, which may be due to the proximity of the photovoltaic site area to roads, having a significant impact on the resistance surface.

## _3.2.3. Construction of ecological corridors based on LCP model_

Based on the LCP model, 105 potential ecological corridors were identified (Fig. 6a). The results of two ecological corridor groups are obtained according to whether they are affected by photovoltaics. The impact of PV site selection on potential ecological corridors is shown in Fig. 6b.

The gravity model was subsequently employed to analyze the interaction intensity between the ecological sources, with significant differences in the forces between patches observed. According to the interaction matrix between pairwise ecological patches computed by Gravity Model, 32 ecological corridors were extracted from 105 (with the threshold of 30%). ## _3.3. Effects of PV projects on the ecological networks_

## _3.3.1. Effects on corridor patency_

The construction of the Photovoltaic projects reduced the corridor patency between the ecological sources, which is reflected in the increases in the LCD value of corridors. All potential ecological corridors have increased the LCD value after being affected by Photovoltaic projects. Table A3 (see Appendix) shows that 61.00% of the potential ecological corridor LCD value increases by no more than 25% after being affected by photovoltaic site selection, and the LCD value growth rate for 32.38% of the corridors is between 25% and 35%. Among those corridors, the one with the smallest increase rate connects patch 12 and patch 13, only increased by 5.48%. This corridor does not pass through the PV site area, so it is less affected. However, the LCD value of the corridor most affected rose by 56.69% (corridor3–7), showing that the degree of photovoltaic impact on the ecological corridors in the study area varies significantly from one another.

## _3.3.2. Effects on corridor length_

In the study of effects on corridor length, the important ecological corridors were taken as the main object. In order to more comprehensively analyze the effects of PV projects on the length of corridors, a total of 39 ecological corridors were selected for research. Of these, 25 are important ecological corridors in both cases, 7 are no longer important ecological corridors without PV projects, and the remaining 7 become important ecological corridors with PV projects. A comparison of the changes in the length of the

ecological corridors is shown in Fig. 7. It can be seen that the PV projects have, on average, shortened most of the corridor length by about 1.33 km. Only four of them increased in length, and all of them increased by less than 5%. The remaining 35 corridors were reduced in length by various levels. The maximum rate of decrease reached 26.17% (no. 1-no.3), which was decreased by 13.24 km, and the minimum rate of decrease was 0.16% (no. 3-no.12), which was decreased by 0.05 km.

## _3.3.3. Effects on connection strength_

All potential ecological corridors were selected in the study of effects on connection strength. A comparison of the rates of variation of ecological corridors’ connection strength with and without PV projects is shown in Fig. 8. It can be seen that 37 ecological corridors have enhanced their connection strength, while the remaining 68 have weakened. Among the enhanced corridors, the maximum rate reached 2115.38% (corridor 5–11), while the minimum rate was 1.623% (corridor 2–14). Among the weakened corridors, the maximum rate reached 96.02% (corridor7–9) while the minimum rate was 2.447% (corridor 10–14). After classifying the enhanced and weakened corridors with natural break classification into five levels (Fig. 9), it can be found that the magnitude of the enhanced ecological corridors is much larger than that of the weakened ones. As can be seen from the distribution figure, the ecological corridors with enhanced connection strength are primarily concentrated in the three middle classes, while the weakened ones are evenly distributed in the five classes.

## **4. Discussion**

## _4.1. Effects of PV projects on the ecological networks_

Ecological corridors serve various purposes, including preserving biodiversity, filtering contaminants, erosion prevention, and flood management. They can also serve as a habitat for wildlife and operate as a conduit, source, sink, barrier, and filter for biological movement (RTT, 1995). Due to the lack of an ecological purpose, PV project construction will impact the existing ecological corridors. For example, the change in soil properties, destruction of vegetation, light pollution, and microclimate influence will negatively impact the migration corridors of different species, leading to the fragmentation of ecological networks and reducing the quality of ecological services.

PV arrays use an inverter to convert the DC power generated by the PV panels into AC power. A PV infrastructure comprises a series of PV panel arrays, inverters, mounts, cabling, monitoring equipment, substation, and access tracks (Guerin, 2017). Therefore, PV project infrastructure may fragment habitats and serve as linear barriers to the movement patterns of certain wildlife species (Hernandez et al., 2014). It significantly fragments the landscape, isolates species, and cuts the entire landscape into isolated parts. Fragmentation may exacerbate the negative effects on species and ecosystems by reducing a species’ capacity to adapt or move. It is detrimental to the integrity of ecological systems and the long-term viability of connected wildlife (Ewers and Didham, 2006).

Due to the installation of PV projects infrastructure, such as PV panels or modules that are then lined up into arrays, PV projects negatively influence the patency, length, and connection strength of the ecological corridors. The construction changed the direction of the corridors between the source patches in the landscape–which hindered species migration and spread and decreased the corridor’s patency (Kuvlesky et al., 2007). Species can travel a greater distance across the permeable landscape than through the landscape with

## high resistance (Avon and Berg`es, 2016).

According to the previous study, when the species has to migrate over high resistance areas, the corridor length increases simultaneously (Ravikumar and Sinha, 2017). However, different from previous research, this study adds a photovoltaic buffer factor to the elements of the resistance surface to replace the actual ecological impact changes and proposes ecological corridor selection to avoid risks. As a result, the length of most of these ecological corridors has decreased.

To conclude, protecting existing ecological corridors and constructing new ones in appropriate locations should be prioritized. According to the location, corridors connected with patches in the southwest corner (no.7, no.8, no.9) are affected most significantly, followed by the northwest (no.5, no.10, no.11, no.12), north and northeast (no.6, no.13, no.14, no.15), and middle patches (no.1). According to the area size (Fig. 4), ecological corridors generated by patches of the medium and small area were more affected, of the large area were moderately affected, and of the super large area were least affected. According to the length, short ecological corridors are affected more than long ones. However, the two most affected are relatively longer (no.1-no.3 and no.8-no.15).

According to the connective strength, corridors connected with patches no.1, no.6, no.8, and no.9 have the most distinguished change; According to the cumulative resistance value, corridors connected with patches no.3, no.7, no.9 have the most distinguished change; According to the corridor length, corridors connected with patches no.5, no.8 have the most distinguished change.

## _4.2. Comparison between the current study with previous results_

This study focuses on ecological corridors to better reflect the landscape pattern and ecological structure. In view of the ecological impact of PV projects, there are some differences in research objectives, methods, and results between this study and previous studies. Previous studies primarily focused on specific effects of photovoltaic projects, such as air pollution, soil erosion, and vegetation loss by qualitative judgments (Zarzavilla et al., 2022). Our purpose is to quantitatively evaluate the ecological impact of PV projects on the ecological corridor and the ecosystem with the GIS analysis.

In the study of ecological corridors, there are many studies related to the influence of natural conditions, hydrologic cycle, and wind power projects. The landscape pattern were extensively analyzed in the context of hydrologic cycle change and revealed the influences of anthropogenic activity on ecosystems (Wu et al., 2017, 2020). The wind power project not only significantly increased the resistance to the formation of ecological corridors at the landscape level, but also had an apparent cutting effect on the landscape (Ravikumar and Sinha, 2017). However, the research on the relationship between PV project location and ecological corridors is still blank.

In addition, most of the previous studies on ecological corridors are based on reality and summarize experiences from completed projects and ecological damage. This study prioritizes considering the impact of photovoltaics on the resistance surface, predicts the ecological impact of photovoltaic power stations, and proposes the selection of ecological corridors to avoid risks before construction.

## _4.3. Implication and application of the results_

The construction of an ecological corridor is beneficial for the conservation of biodiversity. Conventional PV site selection usually ignores the impact on ecological corridors, so this study improves the factors to be considered in future PV construction.

Construction of projects at different stages can have various effects on ecosystems (Hazem and Breesam, 2019; Lin, 2018). In order to reduce the negative impact of a PV project on the landscape ecology, an environmental impact assessment should be carried out strictly to scientifically plan and identify the optimal location for PV projects before construction. Corridors have significant changes in patency, length, and connection strength after PV projects construction. Large-scale PV projects should be avoided in ecologically sensitive areas to minimize the impact on the ecosystem. After construction, ecological restoration should be carried out correctly to improve the ecosystem service functions and maintain biodiversity.

In addition, reducing carbon emissions by replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy has received increasing attention in most countries. In the meantime, measures are still required to mitigate the environmental and ecological impacts caused by renewable energy development (HONG et al., 2014). It can be foreseen that there will be a large number of large-scale photovoltaic projects in China in the future. This study is conducive to guiding the site selection of future photovoltaic projects.

## _4.4. Limitation and future study_

In this study, the scope of the photovoltaic site selection area is much smaller than the ecological corridor construction area, and the research scope is relatively limited. Secondly, only the patency, length, and connection strength of ecological corridors were calculated, and most of them were based on cutting linear ecological corridors by blocking photovoltaic project facilities. Specific aspects, such as the impact of grass installations on soil structure, chemical properties, and air pollution, have not been considered.

In addition, since no PV projects are already built in this area, we use the PV project as a prediction buffer. Nevertheless, the weight of the photovoltaic buffer factor is inaccurate or inconsistent with reality. For instance, photovoltaic projects will simultaneously affect vegetation coverage and land types during operation, so the entire project cannot be taken as a buffer factor in isolation. The conclusions of the research may contain errors. In future research, the simulation results can be improved by expanding the research area and combining it with the actual construction situation.

attention. This paper studied the impacts of PV projects on the ecosystems in Quzhou City, Zhejiang Province of China. A research framework (Fig. 2) was proposed to construct the ecological networks by the LCD and LCP models. It takes the data of NDVI, DEM, and OSM to support the identification of ecological sources and construction of resistance surfaces. The PV buffer factor was incorporated into the LCD and LCP models as an indicator for resistance surface to quantify the impact of PV on potential ecological corridor patency, length, and connection strength.

The conclusions of the study are as follows:1) A total of 15 ecological sources are identified through the change of NDVI values between 2014 and 2020 in the research area (1 source patch under 0.5 km[2] , 12 source patches between 0.5 and 5 km[2] , and 2 source patches over 5 km[2] ). 2) Based on the LCP model and Gravity Model, 32 ecological corridors were extracted from the total 105 corridors. 3) PV projects have different degrees of impact on the patency, length, and connection strength of the corridor. The increase in LCD value varies from 5.48% to 56.69%, indicating a decrease in corridor patency. For the connection strength, the most enhanced corridor (5− 11) reached a magnitude of 2115.38%, while the most weakened corridor (7− 9) reached − 96.02%.

The results could improve the diversity and accuracy of quantified assessment for ecological corridors and provide definite recommendations for PV project site selection. Furthermore, it donated a new approach for regional ecological network security pattern construction, optimization, and PV site selection.
